newsitem.title: BRAZIL: New Banespa deal won't derail sell-off -- analysts.
newsitem.headline: New Banespa deal won't derail sell-off -- analysts.

text.p: The Brazilian government has not abandoned long-term plans to privatize troubled state bank Banespa despite a new deal that could allow Sao Paulo state to retain control of the bank, analysts said.
The possibility of returning the bank to state control is widely viewed as a sweetener that would make the deal politically acceptable to Sao Paulo state lawmakers.
However, analysts said the terms of the deal, expected to be announced this week, virtually ensured the bank's privatization.
"Sao Paulo state is not in any financial shape to recover Banespa," said former Central Bank official Alberto Furuguem.
"Making Banespa a federal bank in the first phase and then privatizing it is the most viable solution," Furuguem said.

State and federal officials are expected to unveil a deal allowing the federal government to take over management of Banespa under a major refinancing package that embraces all of Sao Paulo state's mammoth 37 billion real debt -- including the 20 billion reais owed to Banespa.

Brazil's largest state bank, Banespa has been under Central Bank administration since December 1994 due to the problems caused by Sao Paulo state's towering debt to the bank. The bank has 1,500 branches and employs 27,000 workers.

Under the new plan, Sao Paulo would pay off 20 percent of its total 37 billion real debt through asset sales. The remainder would be refinanced over 30 years at an interest rate of six percent plus inflation.
Included in the package would be all of Sao Paulo state's debt: to state banks Banespa and Nossa Caixa Nosso Banco, outstanding debt in the form of public securities, and more.
The terms of the package are similar to deals already reached in September with Minas Gerais and Rio Grande do Sul states, for 8.6 billion reais and 6.0 billion reais respectively.

But unlike those deals, the Sao Paulo pact would also require the transfer of state bank Banespa to federal government hands. Sao Paulo would be allowed to regain control of the bank after one year only if it had paid off half of its 20 billion real debt to Banespa, according to sources close to the deal.
And analysts said it was doubtful bankrupt Sao Paulo state would be able to put together the necessary amount -- estimated at around 10 billion reais -- within 12 months.

Antonio Madeira, analyst at MCM consulting, said the provision allowing Sao Paulo to regain control of the bank, though largely meaningless, would smooth passage of the deal through Congress by lawmakers who might otherwise block it.
"This is one of those cases in which the solution is political," said Madeira.
While the transfer of the bank to federal control is seen as key to any deal, a former Banespa president is leading a campaign to torpedo it and keep the bank in Sao Paulo state's hands.
"I am fighting to remove this item from the deal," said Carlos Augusto Meinberg, who ran Banespa before the Central Bank took over the bank in December 1994.

Like many analysts, Meinberg believes the federal government's long-term aim is to retain control of the bank and eventually privatise it. Analysts believe the federal government wants to privatize Banespa, but has refrained from saying so publicly for political reasons.

Meinberg said Banespa should remain under state control and continue as a development bank. He added that the federal government's deal with Sao Paulo should be modeled after agreements with Rio Grande do Sul, in which the state was allowed to refinance its debt without giving up control of its bank, Banrisul.
